explanation_result.explanation:
The upward pressure on coffee prices in early April 2021 was driven by a combination of severe weather disruptions in key growing regions, major global freight bottlenecks, and shrinking inventories alongside expected demand recovery.

First, drought in Brazil—the world's largest producer—significantly reduced crop expectations for 2021, with potential output losses estimated at up to 50% (source: doc_b6b918e784a00364, doc_df65c8512f25a1e1, doc_8af357674f52e082, doc_b46fca10aa7a9c5a). At the same time, torrential rains threatened crops in Colombia, the second-largest producer (source: doc_8af357674f52e082, doc_b46fca10aa7a9c5a, doc_e41ea6047c59a104).

Second, global supply chain disruptions created severe delivery delays. A shortage of shipping containers, rising freight costs from Latin America (more than doubling to tripling), and the blockage in the Suez Canal severely limited bean transport (source: doc_b6b918e784a00364, doc_df65c8512f25a1e1, doc_8903964e9872a5f6, doc_3561ea4460d7640a).

Finally, U.S. coffee stockpiles had fallen to six-year lows, and Marex Spectron projected a global coffee deficit of up to 10.7 million bags, leaving the market highly vulnerable to price rallies as COVID-19 restrictions eased and demand began to rebound (source: doc_b6b918e784a00364, doc_df65c8512f25a1e1, doc_8af357674f52e082, doc_b46fca10aa7a9c5a, doc_e41ea6047c59a104).
